name: Portuguese (European)
variety: Standard European Portuguese as spoken in Lisbon (the variety of the IPA Handbook illustration)
sources: Cruz-Ferreira, Madalena (1995). European Portuguese. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 25(2), 90-94. Reprinted in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association (1999), Cambridge University Press.
Mateus, Maria Helena and d'Andrade, Ernesto (2000). The Phonology of Portuguese. Oxford University Press.

Escudero, Paola; Boersma, Paul; Rauber, Andréia Schurt; Bion, Ricardo A. H. (2009). A cross-dialect acoustic description of vowels: Brazilian and European Portuguese. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 126(3), 1379-1393.
Frota, Sónia and Vigário, Marina (2001). On the correlates of rhythmic distinctions: the European/Brazilian Portuguese case. Probus 13, 247-275.
Frota, Sónia (2000). Prosody and Focus in European Portuguese: Phonological Phrasing and Intonation. New York: Garland.
Frota, Sónia (2014). The intonational phonology of European Portuguese. In Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology II. Oxford University Press.
Vigário, Marina (2003). The Prosodic Word in European Portuguese. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male, Lisbon (means over speakers, stressed oral vowels)
vowel_formants.formants: two values per vowel, F1 and F2; the source does not report F3, and it covers only the seven stressed oral vowels (not [ɐ], [ɨ] or the nasal vowels)

contrasts: four vowel heights under stress: /i e ɛ a/ and /u o ɔ a/ (avô [ɐˈvo] versus avó [ɐˈvɔ], pê versus pé)
/a/ versus /ɐ/ under stress in a few contexts (falámos [fɐˈlamuʃ] past versus falamos [fɐˈlɐmuʃ] present)
oral versus nasal vowels (lá versus lã, mito versus minto) and oral versus nasal diphthongs (pau versus pão, mais versus mães)
tap /ɾ/ versus strong /ʁ/ between vowels (caro versus carro)
four sibilants /s z ʃ ʒ/ in onsets, neutralised to one coda sibilant
lexical stress (dúvida noun versus duvida verb), always accompanied by a change of vowel quality
allophony: unstressed vowels are raised and centralised: /a/ is [ɐ], /e ɛ/ are [ɨ], /o ɔ/ are [u]; only a few unstressed syllables keep a full vowel (before coda /l/ as in Alto, salgar; in diphthongs; in words such as padeiro, corar with historically long vowels)

[ɨ] (a close central to back unrounded vowel, written ɯ by Cruz-Ferreira) is very short and is usually deleted in connected speech, above all word-finally and next to voiceless consonants: telefone [tlɨˈfɔn], desprezar [dʃpɾˈzaɾ], pequeno [ˈpkenu]
final unstressed [u] is short, often devoiced or deleted
word-initial unstressed 'e' before a sibilant is dropped: esperar [ʃpɨˈɾaɾ], estar [ʃtaɾ]; elsewhere initial unstressed 'e' is [i]
in Lisbon /e/ is [ɐ] before palatal consonants (telha [ˈtɐʎɐ], tenho [ˈtɐɲu]) and the diphthong written 'ei' is [ɐj] (leite [ˈlɐjtɨ]); written 'ou' is a monophthong [o]
final '-em', '-ens' is the nasal diphthong [ɐ̃j̃] (bem [bɐ̃j̃], homem [ˈɔmɐ̃j̃])
/b d ɡ/ are fricatives or approximants [β ð ɣ] except after a pause or a nasal (and /d/ after /l/)
/l/ is velarised [ɫ] in all positions, most strongly in the coda; it is never vocalised
the coda sibilant is [ʃ] before a voiceless consonant and before pause, [ʒ] before a voiced consonant, and [z] before a vowel across a word boundary (os amigos [uz ɐˈmiɣuʃ])
strong /ʁ/ is a uvular fricative [ʁ] or [χ], sometimes a uvular trill [ʀ]; an alveolar trill [r] survives with older and regional speakers; coda /ɾ/ is a tap, often devoiced or dropped before pause

a nasal vowel before a stop is followed by a brief nasal consonant homorganic with the stop (campo [ˈkɐ̃mpu]); before fricatives and at the end of a word there is no nasal consonant (longe [ˈlõʒɨ], fim [fĩ])
a stressed vowel before a nasal onset is not nasalised; stressed /a/ there is [ɐ] (cama [ˈkɐmɐ])
/t d/ are dental and are never affricated before [i]
syllable_structure: (C)(C)V(G)(C) underlyingly, with the coda limited to /l/, /ɾ/, a sibilant or nasality; deletion of [ɨ] produces long surface clusters
phonotactics: onset clusters are stop or /f/ plus /ɾ/ or /l/; other clusters of the spelling (pn, ps, gn, dv) are said without an epenthetic vowel or with a short [ɨ]
/ɾ/, /ɲ/ and /ʎ/ do not begin native words; strong /ʁ/ occurs word-initially, after /n l s/ and between vowels (rr)
nasal vowels do not contrast before a nasal onset consonant
connected speech: vowel deletion, and fusion of vowels across word boundaries (a + a gives [a], casa amarela [ˈkazamɐˈɾɛlɐ])

stress.type: lexical, restricted to the last three syllables
stress.rule: Stress is penultimate in words ending in a, e, o (also with s, m, ns), final in words ending in l, r, z, i, u, a nasal vowel or a diphthong, and elsewhere (including all antepenultimate stress) it is marked by an accent in the spelling.
stress.cues: vowel quality (full vowels only under stress) and duration; intensity; pitch only where the word carries a pitch accent, which many words in a phrase do not

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: unstressed /a/ is [ɐ], /e ɛ/ are [ɨ], /o ɔ/ are [u]; [ɨ] and final [u] are very short and often deleted
rhythm.notes: Traditionally called stress-timed. Frota and Vigário (2001), using the proportion of vocalic intervals and the variability of consonantal intervals, find mixed rhythm with stress-timed and syllable-timed properties, and a clear difference from Brazilian Portuguese. Escudero et al. (2009) found stressed vowels shorter in European than in Brazilian Portuguese.

length.notes: No length contrast. Vowel fusion across words (a + a) gives an open [a] rather than a long vowel.

intonation.declarative: sparse pitch accents: a high or rising accent (H* or L*+H) on the first stressed syllable of the phrase, then a high stretch with most medial words unaccented, and a falling nuclear accent on the last stressed syllable (H+L*) with a low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: same word order as the statement; falling nuclear accent H+L* followed by a final rise on the post-tonic syllables (LH%); with a final stressed syllable the fall and rise are both squeezed onto it
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, falling nuclear accent H+L* and low boundary, close to the statement contour
intonation.continuation: high boundary (H%, often after a rising accent) at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: nuclear H+L*: high on the syllable before the stress, falling to low within the stressed syllable; prenuclear H* or L*+H
intonation.notes: Frota (2000, 2014). Narrow focus is marked by H*+L on the focused word. The Lisbon standard has far fewer pitch accents per phrase than Brazilian Portuguese or northern European varieties.

phonation: final unstressed [ɨ] and [u] are often devoiced or whispered before pause and next to voiceless consonants

problems: pretonic e is often left unreduced in the first syllable of words of three or more syllables: that syllable is given secondary stress, which blocks the change to [ɨ] unless a spelling rule gives [ɨ] outright (a and o are reduced there). So pequeno is [pˌekˈenʊ], menino [mˌenˈinʊ], felicidade [fˌelisidˈadɨ], perceber [pˌeɾsɨbˈeɾ], where the literature has [pɨˈkenu], [mɨˈninu], [fɨlisiˈðaðɨ], [pɨɾsɨˈbeɾ]
[ɨ] is never deleted (only word-initial 'es' loses its vowel), so the consonant clusters of connected European speech do not arise
final '-em', '-ens' is an oral diphthong plus a velar nasal [eɪŋ] (bem, tem, homem, também, ontem) instead of the nasal diphthong [ɐ̃j̃]; 'ãe' has an oral glide [ɐ̃j]

every nasal vowel is followed by a nasal consonant segment, also before fricatives and at the end of a word (longe [lˈõnʒɨ], ênfase [ˈẽnfɐzɨ], fim [fˈĩŋ], bom [bˈõm]), where the language has a plain nasal vowel
the Lisbon centralisation before palatals is missing: leite, rei have [eɪ] and tenho, espelho, vermelho have [e], against [ɐj] and [ɐ]
stressed 'a' before a nasal onset is nasalised as in Brazilian Portuguese (cama [kˈɐ̃mɐ], falamos [fˌɐlˈɐ̃mʊʃ]); European Portuguese has oral [ɐ]
/b d ɡ/ are always stops; the fricative allophones [β ð ɣ] are missing
/l/ imports the English phoneme, clear before a vowel and dark only in the coda; European /l/ is velarised in all positions
rule errors reduce some stressed vowels: pressa and depressa come out with stressed [ɨ], and quente comes out as [kˈentɨ] without the nasal vowel
final unstressed 'o' is the lax vowel labelled [ʊ], shared with the Brazilian table; European Portuguese has a short [u] that is often devoiced
intonation uses one of the generic tune sets (voice option 'intonation 2'): the sparse accents, the falling nuclear accent H+L* and the fall plus final rise of yes-no questions are not modelled
good: [ɨ] and [ɐ] exist as phonemes; unstressed a and o are reduced everywhere and unstressed e in syllables without secondary stress (telefone [tˌelɨfˈonɨ], falar [fɐlˈaɾ], morar [muɾˈaɾ], Portugal [pˌuɾtuɡˈɑl])
coda sibilants are [ʃ] and [ʒ] by voicing of the next consonant and [z] before a vowel in the next word
strong r is uvular [ʁ] and weak r a tap; coda l is kept as a dark lateral and not vocalised; t and d are not palatalised
word-initial 'es' plus consonant is [ʃ] plus consonant (esperar [ʃpɨɾˈaɾ])
the nasal vowels and the diphthongs [ɐ̃w̃], [õj̃], [ũj̃] are present

notes: The two Portuguese voices share one rule file (pt_rules) with conditional rules; the European voice is the less developed of the two. The formant values are for stressed vowels only; the reduced vowels [ɐ] and [ɨ], which carry most of the difference from Brazilian Portuguese, have no cited values here.
